title: Working at height and ladders
siteNotes: Which ladders, stepladders, platforms and step stools the venue has, where they are kept and who may use which (your manager will show you).
Who is trained to use anything beyond a stepladder, such as towers or mobile platforms.
Who is trained for marquee and event rigging, and the arrangements for contractors.
How ladders are inspected and logged, and who to report damaged equipment to.
Any heights where the venue has said a task must not be done by staff at all.
legalNotes: Avoid work at height where reasonably practicable, use suitable equipment, and make sure people are competent: Work at Height Regulations 2005 (https://www.hse.gov.uk/work-at-height/ and https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/735/contents). The HSE hub page confirmed; the regulation detail was not read in full.

Ladders and stepladders: HSE guidance 'Safe use of ladders and stepladders' (INDG455, replaced by LA455 in July 2021, https://ladderassociation.org.uk/la455/). The HSE page itself could not be loaded. A search summary supported: they suit low-risk, short-duration work (staying up more than 30 minutes at a time suggests different equipment), the ladder must be level and stable and secured where practicable, in safe condition, with a pre-use check each working day.

NOT VERIFIED against the leaflet text: 'three points of contact' and 'never overreach' are standard HSE ladder advice but I could not read the exact wording. The 'tie, inspect, level' memory aid is not a phrase I could confirm in the leaflet; the slides teach the underlying points (secure, check, level footing) without presenting it as a quote.
No heights or weights are quoted, deliberately.
Fall from any height can cause serious injury: general HSE position, widely stated; not quoted from a specific page.

Review 6 Oct 2026: HSE/Ladder Association LA455 (July 2021, replaced INDG455; no later replacement found) re-checked via the Ladder Association copy: three points of contact; do not stand on the top platform or upper steps of a stepladder; level, stable, pre-use check; do not overreach; keep loads light; stepladders for light, short-duration work (about 30 minutes at a time). Changes: 'Have someone foot it' removed from the Secure step (footing is guidance for leaning ladders as a last resort, not a general stepladder rule) and 'top steps' added to the Do-not list. The 'check, level, secure' memory aid is the session's own, not an HSE phrase.

The legal test in the Work at Height Regulations 2005 is 'avoid where reasonably practicable', then prevent falls, then minimise the distance and consequences. The slide's 'avoid if you can' is a fair plain-English summary. Not verified from the Regulations text this review.

cards.title: Working at height and ladders
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- decide whether a task needs to be done at height at all
- check and use a stepladder safely
- know what you must not do, and who may do what

cards.title: A fall from any height can be serious
cards.body:
Changing a bulb, hanging a decoration or reaching a high shelf all count as working at height. You do not need to be on a roof to be badly hurt.

> The law says to avoid working at height if you can, and to use suitable equipment if you cannot.

items.title: Bulbs and signs
items.text: A quick job still needs the right kit.

items.title: Wedding decor
items.text: Hanging items at a venue or marquee.

cards.title: Can you avoid it?
cards.body: Ask before you reach for a ladder. Can the item be brought down to you, a long-handled tool used or the job done from the floor? If you must go up, use suitable equipment.

items.title: Avoid
items.text: Do it from the ground if you can.

items.title: Right equipment
items.text: Choose kit that suits the task.

items.title: Trained people
items.text: Only if you are competent to use it.

cards.title: Stepladders are for short, light jobs
cards.body:
A stepladder suits short, light tasks. If a job is long, heavy or needs both hands for a long time, a different piece of equipment is needed. HSE guidance suggests thinking again if you would be on a ladder for more than 30 minutes at a time.

**Your manager will show you** what the venue has and who may use it.

tr.title: Light, long
tr.text: Ask for a platform or other kit.

bl.title: Heavy, short
bl.text: Ask. A ladder is not the answer.

br.title: Heavy, long
br.text: Not a ladder job. Ask your manager.

cards.title: Check, level, secure
cards.body: Do these every time, even for a quick job.

items.title: Inspect
items.text: Look for damage, loose feet and missing parts.

items.title: Level
items.text: Firm, flat floor. Fully open and locked.

items.title: Secure
items.text: Stable, not rocking. Do not use it if it wobbles.

items.title: Clear
items.text: Doors, people and spills out of the way.

cards.title: Safe use, and what never to do
cards.body: Keep your balance and keep hold. Move the ladder rather than stretching.

left.title: Do
items: Face the steps and keep three points of contact
Keep your body within the sides
Come down and move it to reach further

right.title: Do not
items: Stand on a chair, box, table or the top steps

cards.title: Only what you are trained for
cards.body:
Some jobs are not for everyone. Marquee and event rigging, working from towers or platforms and anything at roof level is for trained, authorised people only.

If you are unsure, stop and ask. **Your manager will show you** who is trained.

items.title: Low and brief
items.text: Stepladder, if trained and kit checked.

items.title: Higher or longer
items.text: Ask for suitable equipment and a trained person.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Avoid working at height if you can
- Stepladders are for short, light jobs
- Inspect, set up level and stable, and keep three points of contact
- Never use a chair or box, and never overreach
- Only do what you are trained for, and report damaged equipment

cards.q: A light fitting in a corridor needs changing and the stepladder is not in the store. What do you do?
options: Stand on a sturdy chair
Stack two crates and step up carefully
Ask for the right kit first
Stretch across from the stairs
cards.why: Chairs, crates and stairs are not equipment for working at height. Wait for the right kit.

cards.q: If you cannot quite reach, it is safe to lean out a little as long as you hold the steps.
cards.why: Overreaching is how people fall. Climb down and move the stepladder.

cards.q: You are about to use a stepladder. Which of these should you do first?
options: Check it, then set it up level and firm
Carry the heaviest box up with you
Lean it against the wall closed
Set it up on a damp floor to save time
cards.why: Inspect it, then set it up level and stable. A wet or uneven floor risks the ladder slipping.

cards.q: Which TWO are right about marquee or event rigging?
options: Anyone can do it if they are careful
Only trained and authorised people should do it
It is a quick job, so it is fine from a chair
If unsure, stop and ask
A stepladder is always enough
cards.why: Rigging and marquee work needs training. If you are not sure, stop and ask.

cards.q: A job means reaching overhead for a long time with both hands busy. What is the best approach?
options: Do it from a stepladder anyway
Ask if a platform would suit better
Do it in short bursts, skipping the ladder check
Stand on the top step
cards.why: Stepladders are for short, light tasks. Long or two-handed jobs need other equipment.

cards.q: What does keeping three points of contact on a stepladder mean?
options: Both feet and one hand holding on
Standing on the top step with both hands free
Leaning against the wall with your back
Holding the ladder with your teeth
cards.why: Keep both feet and a hand, or both hands and a foot, in contact while you climb and work.

cards.q: A stepladder is a good choice for a long, heavy job as long as you are careful.
cards.why: Stepladders suit short, light tasks. Long or heavy jobs need other equipment.

cards.q: A bulb needs changing above a stairwell. What should you ask first?
options: How quickly can I get up there?
Which chair is the sturdiest?
Can I avoid it, or who is trained?
How high can I lean out?
cards.why: Avoid working at height where you can. If you cannot, use the right equipment and trained people.

cards.q: If a ladder has a loose foot, you should report it and take it out of use.
cards.why: Damaged equipment should not be used. Report it so it is checked or replaced.

cards.q: You cannot reach a decoration from your stepladder. What do you do?
options: Stretch one arm further
Climb down and move the stepladder
Step up onto the top platform
Ask a guest to hold it
cards.why: Never overreach. Come down and reposition the ladder.
